title: GPCRs Activate Trimeric G Proteins
explain: GPCRs contain seven membrane-spanning helices. Ligand binding changes receptor shape, allowing it to activate a heterotrimeric G protein, which can then regulate an effector such as adenylyl cyclase. Figure focus: Trace the diagram left to right: extracellular ligand -> seven-pass receptor -> alpha-beta-gamma G protein -> membrane effector.
mustKnow: GPCRs have seven transmembrane helices.
They interact with a trimeric G protein.
Adenylyl cyclase is a common downstream effector.

terms.meaning: A GTP-binding signaling protein made of alpha, beta, and gamma subunits.
A membrane enzyme that produces cAMP from ATP.
A molecule that binds specifically to a receptor.

diagramGuide: Trace the diagram left to right: extracellular ligand -> seven-pass receptor -> alpha-beta-gamma G protein -> membrane effector.
The nucleotide label is on G-alpha; GDP/GTP exchange changes the state of G-alpha, not the receptor.

interaction.q: Which component directly exchanges GDP for GTP after ligand-bound GPCR activation?
interaction.explanation: The nucleotide-binding alpha subunit is activated by GDP release and GTP binding.

title: Three-Dimensional GPCR Structure
explain: The structural model shows a GPCR as a compact bundle of seven alpha helices crossing the membrane. A ligand approaching the receptor can stabilize a new conformation that is transmitted to the intracellular G-protein-binding side. Figure focus: Count the seven colored alpha-helices forming the compact receptor bundle.
mustKnow: The seven helices form one receptor bundle.
Ligand binding changes receptor conformation.
The conformational change connects outside binding to inside signaling.

terms.meaning: A change in a protein's three-dimensional shape.
An alpha helix that passes through the lipid bilayer.

diagramGuide: Count the seven colored alpha-helices forming the compact receptor bundle.
The small space-filling ligand approaches the extracellular face; signaling is transmitted to the opposite, cytoplasmic face.

interaction.q: A mutation that prevents movement of the cytoplasmic ends of the seven helices would most directly impair binding to which partner?
interaction.explanation: The intracellular face of an activated GPCR couples to the heterotrimeric G protein.

title: GPCR Activation, Amplification, and Attenuation
explain: The diagram follows activation from ligand-bound receptor to G protein and effector. One active receptor can activate multiple G proteins, creating amplification; receptor phosphorylation and arrestin binding then stop further activation. Figure focus: Follow numbered panels rather than reading by rows: receptor activation precedes G-protein separation and effector activation.
mustKnow: A single active receptor can activate multiple G proteins.
This one-to-many step amplifies the signal.
Phosphorylation plus arrestin produces attenuation.

terms.meaning: Reduction or termination of signaling strength.
A protein that binds an active phosphorylated GPCR and blocks further G-protein activation.
A GPCR kinase that phosphorylates an active receptor.

diagramGuide: Follow numbered panels rather than reading by rows: receptor activation precedes G-protein separation and effector activation.
Green box marks amplification; the upper red box marks GTP-hydrolysis shutoff; the lower red box marks GRK/arrestin attenuation.

interaction.q: Which event belongs to receptor attenuation rather than G-alpha's intrinsic shutoff?
options: Arrestin binding to a GRK-phosphorylated receptor
interaction.explanation: GRK phosphorylation followed by arrestin binding desensitizes the receptor.

title: The GPCR-G Protein Cycle
explain: Ligand-bound GPCR promotes GDP release and GTP binding on G alpha. G alpha-GTP activates an effector such as adenylyl cyclase, which produces cAMP; G alpha then hydrolyzes GTP, reassociates with beta-gamma, and signaling stops. GRK and arrestin further desensitize the receptor. Figure focus: Map each written step to the adjacent cycle on slide 193.
mustKnow: GDP-to-GTP exchange activates G alpha.
Adenylyl cyclase produces cAMP.
GTP hydrolysis deactivates G alpha.
GRK phosphorylation and arrestin block the receptor.

terms.meaning: The nucleotide-binding G-protein subunit that regulates an effector.
Hydrolysis of bound GTP to GDP, switching G alpha off.
Reduced receptor signaling despite continued ligand presence.

diagramGuide: Map each written step to the adjacent cycle on slide 193.
Separate three shutoff events: G-alpha hydrolyzes GTP, subunits reassociate, and GRK/arrestin desensitizes the receptor.

interaction.q: What is the correct order immediately after ligand binding?
options: cAMP production -> receptor binding -> GTP loading
Arrestin binding -> GRK removal -> G-alpha activation
GDP release -> GTP binding -> G-alpha-effector interaction
GTP hydrolysis -> GDP release -> arrestin removal
interaction.explanation: Ligand-bound receptor first promotes nucleotide exchange, then active G-alpha regulates the effector.

title: AMP Compared with Cyclic AMP
explain: Both molecules contain adenine, ribose, and phosphate. In cAMP, the phosphate forms a cyclic linkage on the ribose; this ring structure distinguishes the second messenger from ordinary AMP. Figure focus: Compare the phosphate connections, not the shared adenine and ribose.
mustKnow: cAMP is cyclic adenosine monophosphate.
Its phosphate forms a cyclic bond with ribose.
cAMP acts as an intracellular second messenger.

terms.meaning: Cyclic adenosine monophosphate, an intracellular second messenger.
Adenosine monophosphate, a nucleotide with adenine, ribose, and one phosphate.

diagramGuide: Compare the phosphate connections, not the shared adenine and ribose.
AMP has a non-cyclic phosphate; cAMP has a phosphate bridge linking two ribose oxygens.

interaction.q: Which atoms are joined by the phosphate to create the cyclic feature of cAMP?
interaction.explanation: The phosphate forms an intramolecular cyclic linkage on one ribose.

title: cAMP as an Amplifying Second Messenger
explain: A first messenger such as serotonin binds a surface receptor, and the cell produces cAMP inside. cAMP diffuses to intracellular targets and can regulate several activities, allowing one extracellular stimulus to create a broad coordinated response. Figure focus: Read the color key: blue is low cAMP, yellow intermediate, red high.
mustKnow: The ligand is the first messenger.
cAMP is an intracellular second messenger.
Second messengers amplify and distribute the signal.

terms.meaning: The extracellular ligand that binds a receptor.
A small intracellular molecule generated or released after receptor activation.
The sea hare whose neuron is shown in the cAMP imaging example.

diagramGuide: Read the color key: blue is low cAMP, yellow intermediate, red high.
Compare the same Aplysia neuron before 5-HT, at 19 seconds, at 100 seconds, and at 10 minutes to see a transient response.

interaction.q: Which time point in the image shows the strongest widespread cAMP signal?
interaction.explanation: Red/yellow signal is maximal around the 100-second image and declines by 10 minutes.

title: cAMP Cascade in a Liver Cell
explain: Glucagon or epinephrine activates a GPCR, G protein, adenylyl cyclase, cAMP, and protein kinase A. The cascade promotes glycogen breakdown and glucose release, while another branch activates CREB to alter gene transcription. Figure focus: Trace the metabolic branch from receptor to glucose release and the nuclear branch from PKA to CREB.
mustKnow: GPCR activation leads to cAMP and protein kinase A.
The pathway activates glycogen phosphorylase and inhibits glycogen synthase.
The metabolic output is glucose mobilization.
PKA can also activate the transcription factor CREB.

terms.meaning: A cAMP-activated kinase that phosphorylates downstream proteins.
An enzyme that promotes glycogen breakdown.
A transcription factor activated by phosphorylation in the cAMP pathway.
An enzyme that converts cAMP to AMP and helps terminate the signal.

diagramGuide: Trace the metabolic branch from receptor to glucose release and the nuclear branch from PKA to CREB.
Notice opposing phosphorylation effects: phosphorylase kinase/glycogen phosphorylase are activated, whereas glycogen synthase is inhibited.

interaction.q: Which pair is driven in opposite functional directions by PKA-dependent phosphorylation?
interaction.explanation: The cascade promotes glycogen breakdown while inhibiting glycogen synthesis.

title: GPCR Signal Attenuation
explain: GRKs phosphorylate an active GPCR, creating a high-affinity site for arrestin. Arrestin and G proteins compete for the same cytoplasmic receptor cavity, so arrestin binding prevents additional G-protein activation and can promote receptor internalization. Figure focus: Follow the receptor between surface, coated pit, vesicle, and recycling routes.
mustKnow: GRKs phosphorylate active GPCRs.
Arrestin selectively binds the active phosphorylated receptor.
Arrestin blocks G-protein coupling.
Attenuation prevents unlimited signaling.

terms.meaning: Removal of a receptor from the cell surface into an intracellular vesicle.
Mutually exclusive binding of G protein or arrestin to the same receptor region.

diagramGuide: Follow the receptor between surface, coated pit, vesicle, and recycling routes.
GRK phosphorylation enables arrestin binding; arrestin both blocks G-protein access and supports internalization.

interaction.q: Which modification creates the receptor state preferentially recognized by arrestin?
options: GRK-mediated phosphorylation of an active GPCR
interaction.explanation: Arrestin preferentially binds the active receptor after GRK phosphorylation.

title: Cell Survival and Cell Death
explain: This slide opens the next lecture, which examines how cells remain alive or activate controlled death programs. The immediate transition is from signaling pathways to apoptosis. Figure focus: This is a section divider; use the background apoptotic-cell imagery only as context.
mustKnow: Cell survival and cell death are regulated biological outcomes.
Apoptosis is the first cell-death mode introduced.

terms.meaning: Maintenance of cellular functions and resistance to death signals.
Loss of cell viability through regulated or damaging processes.

diagramGuide: This is a section divider; use the background apoptotic-cell imagery only as context.
The examinable transition is from receptor signaling to regulated survival/death decisions.

interaction.q: Which topic immediately follows cellular signaling in the compiled material?
interaction.explanation: Page 199 opens the cell survival and cell death lecture.

title: Apoptosis
explain: The tissue image marks cells with the condensed, rounded appearance associated with apoptosis. Apoptosis is a regulated form of cell death in which a cell dismantles itself in an orderly way. Figure focus: Arrows indicate isolated cells with dark, compact nuclei and reduced cell volume relative to neighbors.
mustKnow: Apoptosis is regulated cell death.
Apoptotic cells show condensation and fragmentation.
Apoptosis removes individual cells in an organized manner.

terms.meaning: A programmed, tightly regulated process of cell self-destruction.
Shrinkage and compacting of an apoptotic cell and its contents.

diagramGuide: Arrows indicate isolated cells with dark, compact nuclei and reduced cell volume relative to neighbors.
Do not identify apoptosis from stain color alone; use condensation, shrinkage, and isolation together.

interaction.q: Which microscopic feature most strongly supports an apoptotic interpretation of the arrowed cells?
interaction.explanation: Apoptotic cells commonly become shrunken with condensed nuclear material.

title: Core Features of Apoptosis
explain: Apoptosis is a controlled cell-death program. The cell and nucleus shrink, the dying cell loses contact with neighboring cells, and the plasma membrane forms surface blebs. Figure focus: Read images A-D as a time sequence ending in fragmentation.
mustKnow: Apoptosis is programmed and orderly.
Cell shrinkage and nuclear shrinkage are characteristic.
Loss of adhesion and membrane blebbing occur.

terms.meaning: An organized program that causes a cell to die.
Formation of rounded bulges on the plasma membrane.

diagramGuide: Read images A-D as a time sequence ending in fragmentation.
The SEM pair emphasizes loss of a smooth outline and formation of membrane blebs.

interaction.q: Which combination is most characteristic of early apoptosis?
options: Cell shrinkage, loss of adhesion, and membrane blebbing
Cell swelling, membrane rupture, and inflammation
DNA replication, spindle assembly, and cytokinesis
interaction.explanation: The slide's images and list emphasize shrinkage, detachment, and blebbing.

title: Final Events in Apoptosis
explain: As apoptosis proceeds, chromatin is cut into small fragments. The cell corpse is then rapidly engulfed by phagocytosis, limiting the release of intracellular material. Figure focus: The electron micrograph shows an apoptotic cell breaking into discrete membrane-bound fragments.
mustKnow: Chromatin becomes fragmented.
The apoptotic corpse is rapidly removed by phagocytosis.

terms.meaning: Breakdown of nuclear DNA-protein material into smaller pieces.
Engulfment and removal of particles or cells by another cell.

diagramGuide: The electron micrograph shows an apoptotic cell breaking into discrete membrane-bound fragments.
Dark compact nuclear material represents chromatin condensation/fragmentation.

interaction.q: The small pieces surrounding the dying cell are best identified as what?
interaction.explanation: Late apoptosis packages cellular material into membrane-bound fragments for clearance.

title: Morphological Sequence of Apoptosis
explain: The diagram shows a normal cell progressing through chromatin condensation, membrane blebbing, nuclear collapse, and formation of membrane-bound apoptotic bodies. Figure focus: Follow arrows clockwise: normal cell -> chromatin condensation -> membrane blebbing/nuclear collapse -> apoptotic bodies.
mustKnow: Chromatin condensation occurs early.
Membrane blebbing precedes apoptotic-body formation.
The dying cell breaks into apoptotic bodies.

terms.meaning: Tight packing of chromatin in the dying nucleus.
A membrane-bound fragment produced by an apoptotic cell.

diagramGuide: Follow arrows clockwise: normal cell -> chromatin condensation -> membrane blebbing/nuclear collapse -> apoptotic bodies.
The final particles retain membrane boundaries, distinguishing orderly packaging from lysis.

interaction.q: Which event occurs immediately before apoptotic-body formation in the depicted sequence?
interaction.explanation: The diagram places blebbing/nuclear collapse just before fragmentation into apoptotic bodies.

title: Clearance of Apoptotic Cells
explain: Apoptotic bodies retain tightly packed organelles and may contain nuclear fragments, all enclosed by an intact membrane. Macrophages engulf them and degrade them in phagolysosomes, so their contents do not spill into surrounding tissue and inflammation is minimal. Figure focus: The micrograph shows a larger phagocyte contacting/engulfing a compact apoptotic body.
mustKnow: Apoptotic bodies remain membrane enclosed.
Macrophages degrade them in phagolysosomes.
Rapid clearance limits inflammation and secondary necrosis.

terms.meaning: A phagocytic immune cell that engulfs cellular debris.
Degradative compartment formed after a phagosome combines with lysosomal machinery.
Loss of membrane integrity when an apoptotic cell is not cleared promptly.

diagramGuide: The micrograph shows a larger phagocyte contacting/engulfing a compact apoptotic body.
Link intact membranes and fast macrophage uptake to minimal leakage and inflammation.

interaction.q: Failure of rapid macrophage clearance would most directly increase the risk of what?
interaction.explanation: Uncleared apoptotic bodies can lose membrane integrity and release contents.

title: Apoptosis Video Reinforcement
explain: This slide provides a linked video intended to reinforce the visible sequence of programmed cell death. Figure focus: The embedded video frame is unavailable in the PDF; treat this as reinforcement, not a new pathway.
mustKnow: Use the video to recognize cell shrinkage, blebbing, fragmentation, and clearance.

terms.meaning: A regulated process that dismantles and removes a cell.

diagramGuide: The embedded video frame is unavailable in the PDF; treat this as reinforcement, not a new pathway.
Recall the morphology sequence from slides 201-204.

interaction.q: Which ordered morphology sequence should the linked apoptosis video reinforce?
interaction.explanation: This is the core visible sequence established by the surrounding apoptosis slides.

title: Apoptosis Animation
explain: This linked animation is a visual review of apoptotic changes and cell removal. Figure focus: The highlighted cell is the intended focus of the animation frame.
mustKnow: An apoptotic cell is dismantled into membrane-bound fragments rather than simply bursting.

terms.meaning: Controlled breakdown of a dying cell into removable parts.

diagramGuide: The highlighted cell is the intended focus of the animation frame.
Use the surrounding epithelial sheet to judge that apoptosis removes individual cells without dissolving the whole tissue.

interaction.q: Why can apoptosis remove one cell from an epithelial sheet with limited damage to neighbors?
options: The apoptotic cell releases digestive enzymes extracellularly
The tissue stops expressing adhesion proteins permanently
The dying cell remains packaged into membrane-bound material
All neighboring cells undergo lysis simultaneously
interaction.explanation: Orderly membrane-contained dismantling limits exposure of neighboring cells.

title: Apoptotic Cell Imaging
explain: The microscopy image shows cells undergoing visible structural changes during apoptosis. Such imaging allows membrane and shape changes to be followed directly. Figure focus: Compare the bright rounded/blebbing cells with the flatter intact cell at left.
mustKnow: Apoptosis can be recognized by characteristic changes in cell morphology.

terms.meaning: The observable shape and structural appearance of a cell.

diagramGuide: Compare the bright rounded/blebbing cells with the flatter intact cell at left.
The fluorescence marks cells as morphology changes; it is not itself a named molecular assay on this slide.

interaction.q: Which observation in live-cell imaging would best distinguish apoptosis from continued proliferation?
options: Formation of two stable spindle poles
Increase in colony size without shape change
interaction.explanation: Rounding and blebbing are visible apoptotic morphology, unlike mitotic progression alone.

title: Extrinsic Apoptosis Pathway
explain: In the receptor-mediated pathway, TNF binds TNFR1. The activated receptor recruits TRADD, FADD, and procaspase-8 into a membrane-associated complex. Procaspase-8 becomes active caspase-8, which activates executioner caspases. Figure focus: Read top to bottom: TNF/TNFR1 -> death-domain adaptors -> procaspase-8 -> initiator caspase-8 -> executioner caspases.
mustKnow: The extrinsic pathway begins at a death receptor.
TNFR1 recruits TRADD, FADD, and procaspase-8.
Caspase-8 is the initiator caspase in this pathway.
Executioner caspases carry out cell dismantling.

terms.meaning: A TNF receptor that can initiate extrinsic apoptosis.
An adaptor that helps recruit procaspase-8.
The initiator caspase activated in the extrinsic pathway.

diagramGuide: Read top to bottom: TNF/TNFR1 -> death-domain adaptors -> procaspase-8 -> initiator caspase-8 -> executioner caspases.
TRADD and FADD are adaptors; they are not the proteases that execute cleavage.

interaction.q: Which complex component provides protease activity first in the extrinsic pathway?
interaction.explanation: TRADD and FADD are adaptors; procaspase-8 becomes the initiator protease caspase-8.

title: BCL-2 Family Controls Mitochondrial Permeability
explain: BCL-2-family proteins form a survival-versus-death switch. Anti-apoptotic members oppose BAX and BAK, while BH3-only proteins promote their activation. Activated BAX and BAK oligomerize in the mitochondrial outer membrane and cause MOMP. Figure focus: Use the left domain diagrams to sort anti-apoptotic, multidomain pro-apoptotic, and BH3-only groups.
mustKnow: BCL-2, BCL-XL, MCL-1, BCL-w, and A1 are anti-apoptotic.
BAX, BAK, and BOK are pro-apoptotic.
BH3-only proteins include BID, BIM, NOXA, and BAD.
BAX/BAK oligomerization causes MOMP.

terms.meaning: Mitochondrial outer-membrane permeabilization.
Pro-apoptotic proteins that form membrane-permeabilizing oligomers.
Upstream apoptosis inducers that activate or release pro-apoptotic BCL-2-family activity.
An anti-apoptotic protein that opposes mitochondrial permeabilization.

diagramGuide: Use the left domain diagrams to sort anti-apoptotic, multidomain pro-apoptotic, and BH3-only groups.
In the right network, BCL-2 inhibits BAX/BAK while BH3-only proteins either activate BAX/BAK or neutralize BCL-2; MOMP releases cytochrome c.

interaction.q: Which set contains only BH3-only pro-apoptotic regulators?
interaction.explanation: The slide lists BID, BIM, NOXA, and BAD among BH3-only apoptosis inducers.

title: Intrinsic Apoptosis Pathway
explain: Cellular stress activates pro-apoptotic BCL-2-family proteins such as BAX. Mitochondria release cytochrome c, which combines with Apaf-1 and procaspase-9. Activated caspase-9 then activates executioner caspases. Figure focus: Read top to bottom: internal damage -> Bax at mitochondrion -> cytochrome-c release -> Apaf-1/procaspase-9 complex -> executioner caspases.
mustKnow: The intrinsic pathway is mitochondria mediated.
MOMP releases cytochrome c into the cytosol.
Cytochrome c, Apaf-1, and procaspase-9 form the activation complex.
Caspase-9 activates executioner caspases.

terms.meaning: A mitochondrial protein that promotes apoptosome formation after release into the cytosol.
A cytosolic scaffold that recruits procaspase-9.
The initiator caspase of the intrinsic pathway.

diagramGuide: Read top to bottom: internal damage -> Bax at mitochondrion -> cytochrome-c release -> Apaf-1/procaspase-9 complex -> executioner caspases.
The mitochondrion is upstream of caspase-9 in the intrinsic pathway.

interaction.q: Which complex activates the intrinsic-pathway initiator caspase?
options: Cyclin B, CDK1, E2F, and pRb
interaction.explanation: Cytochrome c released from mitochondria assembles with Apaf-1 and procaspase-9.

title: Detecting Apoptosis with Annexin V
explain: Healthy cells keep phosphatidylserine on the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane. During apoptosis it moves to the outer leaflet, where it acts as an eat-me signal. Annexin V binds exposed phosphatidylserine and can therefore mark apoptotic cells. Figure focus: Compare leaflet position of phosphatidylserine in normal versus apoptotic membrane cartoons.
mustKnow: Phosphatidylserine is normally on the cytoplasmic leaflet.
Apoptosis exposes phosphatidylserine on the cell surface.
Annexin V detects exposed phosphatidylserine.

terms.meaning: A phospholipid-binding protein used to detect exposed phosphatidylserine.
A membrane phospholipid that becomes an external eat-me signal during apoptosis.
A surface cue that promotes phagocytic clearance.

diagramGuide: Compare leaflet position of phosphatidylserine in normal versus apoptotic membrane cartoons.
Annexin V binds only after PS becomes exposed on the extracellular leaflet.

interaction.q: An Annexin-V-positive cell most directly indicates which membrane change?
options: Phosphatidylserine exposure on the outer leaflet
interaction.explanation: Annexin V recognizes phosphatidylserine after its apoptotic externalization.

title: Detecting Cytochrome c Release
explain: BAX/BAK pores compromise the mitochondrial outer membrane and release cytochrome c. In healthy cells, cytochrome c staining is confined to mitochondria; after apoptosis induction, its staining becomes diffuse throughout the cytosol. Figure focus: Untreated cells show punctate/reticular green mitochondrial cytochrome c; treated cells show diffuse green cytosolic signal.
mustKnow: BAX/BAK pores release cytochrome c.
Diffuse cytochrome c staining indicates mitochondrial release.
Staurosporine is used here to induce apoptosis.

terms.meaning: A compound commonly used experimentally to induce apoptosis.
A spread-out staining pattern consistent with release from mitochondria.

diagramGuide: Untreated cells show punctate/reticular green mitochondrial cytochrome c; treated cells show diffuse green cytosolic signal.
Blue nuclei are a positional reference, not the apoptosis readout.

interaction.q: Which fluorescence pattern indicates mitochondrial outer-membrane permeabilization?
options: Absence of any green signal in all cells
interaction.explanation: Cytochrome c changes from mitochondrial puncta to a diffuse distribution after release.

title: Apoptosis Detection Video
explain: This linked video reinforces experimental detection of apoptotic cells. Figure focus: The embedded video is reinforcement for apoptotic morphology.
mustKnow: Annexin V detects external phosphatidylserine, while diffuse cytochrome c indicates mitochondrial release.

terms.meaning: A measurable change used to identify cells undergoing apoptosis.

diagramGuide: The embedded video is reinforcement for apoptotic morphology.
Use shrinkage, blebbing, fragmentation, and loss of attachment as the observable criteria.

interaction.q: Which feature would be least consistent with apoptosis in the linked microscopy?
options: Immediate rupture with widespread cellular swelling
interaction.explanation: Swelling and abrupt rupture are more typical of necrotic damage than orderly apoptosis.

title: Cell Cycle and Mitosis Overview
explain: The eukaryotic cell cycle contains interphase—G1, S, and G2—and M phase. DNA and cellular components are duplicated during interphase. Mitosis separates chromosomes, and cytokinesis divides one cell into two genetically identical diploid daughter cells. Figure focus: Read the cycle clockwise G1 -> S -> G2 -> M -> cytokinesis.
mustKnow: Interphase consists of G1, S, and G2.
DNA is replicated before mitosis.
Mitosis partitions chromosomes.
Cytokinesis physically divides the cell.

terms.meaning: Nuclear division that produces genetically equivalent chromosome sets.
Physical division of the cell into two daughters.
G1, S, and G2 phases between cell divisions.

diagramGuide: Read the cycle clockwise G1 -> S -> G2 -> M -> cytokinesis.
Keep chromosome partitioning (mitosis) distinct from physical cell splitting (cytokinesis).

interaction.q: Which event belongs to cytokinesis rather than mitosis?
options: Physical division of the cytoplasm into two cells
Alignment of chromosomes at the spindle midplane
interaction.explanation: Cytokinesis partitions the cell body after chromosome segregation.

title: Purposes of Mitosis
explain: Mitosis increases cell number during growth, replaces damaged or worn-out cells, and enables asexual reproduction in organisms such as yeast. Propidium iodide can stain DNA for analysis. Figure focus: Panel A is the phase wheel; panel B links DNA/chromosome form to phase; the histogram is DNA-content measurement after propidium iodide staining.
mustKnow: Mitosis supports growth and development.
Mitosis replaces and repairs cells.
Mitosis can support asexual reproduction.
Propidium iodide stains DNA.

terms.meaning: A fluorescent DNA-binding stain.
Production of offspring without fusion of gametes.

diagramGuide: Panel A is the phase wheel; panel B links DNA/chromosome form to phase; the histogram is DNA-content measurement after propidium iodide staining.
A replicated chromosome has two cohesin-linked sister chromatids but is still counted as one chromosome until separation.

interaction.q: A propidium-iodide histogram peak at twice the G1 DNA content is most enriched for cells in which state?
interaction.explanation: Cells have doubled DNA after S phase and retain it through G2 until division.

title: Interphase and G0
explain: Interphase occupies most of the cell cycle. G1 supports growth and organelle production, S phase replicates nuclear DNA, and G2 prepares proteins and energy for division. Cells that stop cycling can enter the quiescent G0 state. Figure focus: Use the circular diagram to place DNA replication in S and chromosome segregation in M.
mustKnow: G1: growth and organelle duplication.
S: DNA replication and sister-chromatid formation.
G2: final preparation for division.
G0: temporary or permanent cell-cycle exit.

terms.meaning: A non-dividing, quiescent state outside the active cycle.
The phase in which nuclear DNA is replicated.
The two replicated copies of one chromosome.

diagramGuide: Use the circular diagram to place DNA replication in S and chromosome segregation in M.
G0 branches from the proliferative cycle rather than forming part of G1-S-G2-M progression.

interaction.q: Which phase produces sister chromatids?
interaction.explanation: Nuclear DNA replication during S phase duplicates each chromosome.

title: DNA State Across G1, S, and G2
explain: In G1, each chromosome contains one linear double-stranded DNA molecule. S phase replicates it. In G2, each chromosome has two sister chromatids held together by cohesins. Figure focus: The text contrasts one unreplicated chromosome in G1 with two cohesin-linked sister chromatids after S.
mustKnow: A G1 chromosome has one DNA double helix.
S phase duplicates the chromosome.
G2 sister chromatids are held together by cohesins.

terms.meaning: A protein complex that holds replicated sister chromatids together.
A less compact chromosome state typical of interphase.

diagramGuide: The text contrasts one unreplicated chromosome in G1 with two cohesin-linked sister chromatids after S.
The dark video rectangle adds no independent label; the testable feature is DNA state across G1, S, and G2.

interaction.q: What physically holds newly replicated sister chromatids together in G2?
interaction.explanation: The slide identifies cohesins as the linkage between sister chromatids.

title: Chromosome Movement During Mitosis
explain: Mitosis depends on interactions between spindle microtubules and chromosome kinetochores. Chromosomes condense in prophase, spindle microtubules attach in prometaphase, chromosomes align at the midplane in metaphase, and sister chromatids move to opposite poles in anaphase. Figure focus: In the right diagram, homologous chromosomes replicate independently; mitosis separates sister chromatids, not homologous pairs.
mustKnow: Kinetochores connect chromosomes to spindle microtubules.
Metaphase chromosomes align at the spindle midplane.
Anaphase separates sister chromatids toward opposite poles.

terms.meaning: A chromosome protein structure that binds spindle microtubules.
The microtubule-based apparatus that separates chromosomes.
Stage when spindle microtubules gain access to and attach to chromosomes.

diagramGuide: In the right diagram, homologous chromosomes replicate independently; mitosis separates sister chromatids, not homologous pairs.
In the microscopy sequence, chromosomes condense, attach to spindle, align at the midplane, then move to opposite poles.

interaction.q: During ordinary mitosis, which structures separate from one another?
interaction.explanation: Mitosis partitions replicated sister chromatids into daughter cells.

title: Mitosis Video Reinforcement
explain: This linked video reviews chromosome condensation, alignment, separation, and formation of daughter cells. Figure focus: Cyan fibers are spindle microtubules; yellow structures are chromosomes/DNA.
mustKnow: The mitotic sequence is prophase, prometaphase, metaphase, anaphase, and telophase, followed by cytokinesis.

terms.meaning: The ordered stages that partition duplicated chromosomes.

diagramGuide: Cyan fibers are spindle microtubules; yellow structures are chromosomes/DNA.
Identify stage from chromosome position relative to spindle poles, not from cell shape alone.

interaction.q: In the fluorescence image, the cyan structures radiating from poles are what?
interaction.explanation: The cyan arrays form the mitotic spindle around the yellow chromosomes.

title: Prophase
explain: During prophase, chromosomes condense and become visible as paired sister chromatids. Compaction reduces chromosome length and increases thickness, while transcription largely shuts down. Centrosomes move apart and the mitotic spindle forms; nuclear-envelope breakdown follows at the end of this transition. Figure focus: Compare diffuse interphase chromatin in the top micrograph with thick individualized prophase chromosomes below.
mustKnow: Chromosomes condense in prophase.
Each replicated chromosome contains two sister chromatids.
Transcription is reduced as chromatin compacts.
The mitotic spindle begins to form.

terms.meaning: Compaction that makes chromosomes shorter, thicker, and visibly distinct.
A microtubule-organizing structure that helps form spindle poles.

diagramGuide: Compare diffuse interphase chromatin in the top micrograph with thick individualized prophase chromosomes below.
The nuclear envelope breaks down late in prophase/prometaphase while centrosomes organize the spindle.

interaction.q: Which event is associated with chromosome condensation during prophase?
options: Displacement of transcription factors and reduced transcription
interaction.explanation: Condensation reduces DNA accessibility and transcriptional activity.

title: Metaphase and Kinetochore Attachment
explain: At metaphase, chromosomes align at the cell equator. Spindle microtubules connect to kinetochores assembled on each chromatid. Kinetochore-associated motors, including dynein, contribute to chromosome movement on the spindle. Figure focus: The micrograph shows chromosomes concentrated at one equatorial plate between opposite spindle poles.
mustKnow: Metaphase chromosomes align at the equator.
Microtubules attach through kinetochores.
Dynein can help move chromosomes along spindle microtubules.

terms.meaning: The equatorial plane where chromosomes align.
A microtubule motor involved in chromosome movement.

diagramGuide: The micrograph shows chromosomes concentrated at one equatorial plate between opposite spindle poles.
Spindle microtubules attach through kinetochores assembled at sister chromatids.

interaction.q: What is the direct chromosome attachment site for spindle microtubules?
interaction.explanation: Kinetochores are protein assemblies on centromeric chromatin that bind spindle microtubules.

title: Spindle Attachment Video
explain: This linked video reinforces how spindle microtubules attach to kinetochores and position chromosomes. Figure focus: The frame is labeled metaphase; chromosome alignment at the equator is the diagnostic feature.
mustKnow: Kinetochore attachment connects chromosome movement to the mitotic spindle.

terms.meaning: Binding of spindle microtubules to chromosome kinetochores.

diagramGuide: The frame is labeled metaphase; chromosome alignment at the equator is the diagnostic feature.
Do not confuse metaphase alignment with anaphase poleward separation.

interaction.q: Which chromosome arrangement identifies the stage shown?
options: Diffuse chromatin in an intact nucleus
interaction.explanation: A metaphase plate at the equator is diagnostic of metaphase.

title: Anaphase, Telophase, and Cytokinesis
explain: In anaphase, sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles. During telophase, a nuclear membrane forms around each chromosome set. Cytokinesis then pinches the cell into two daughter cells. Figure focus: Top micrograph: sister chromatids move toward opposite poles in anaphase. Bottom: chromosome sets are at poles and nuclei reform in telophase.
mustKnow: Anaphase separates sister chromatids.
Telophase rebuilds daughter nuclei.
Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm.

terms.meaning: Mitotic stage in which sister chromatids move apart.
Stage in which chromosome sets are enclosed in new nuclei.
Division of one cell into two daughter cells.

diagramGuide: Top micrograph: sister chromatids move toward opposite poles in anaphase. Bottom: chromosome sets are at poles and nuclei reform in telophase.
The cleavage furrow/cell pinching belongs to cytokinesis, which overlaps late telophase.

interaction.q: Which event distinguishes telophase from anaphase?
options: Attachment of kinetochores to spindle fibers
Reformation of nuclear membranes around chromosome sets
interaction.explanation: Nuclear envelopes re-form in telophase after chromosomes reach the poles.

title: Mitosis Completion Video
explain: This linked video reviews the final mitotic stages and physical separation of daughter cells. Figure focus: The frame is labeled prophase and shows condensed material within one cell.
mustKnow: Nuclear re-formation occurs in telophase, while cell separation occurs by cytokinesis.

terms.meaning: One of the two cells produced by division of a parent cell.

diagramGuide: The frame is labeled prophase and shows condensed material within one cell.
At this stage chromosomes are becoming visible but have not formed a metaphase plate.

interaction.q: Which stage should follow the prophase frame before anaphase begins?
interaction.explanation: Chromosomes next attach and align during prometaphase/metaphase before separating.

title: Discovery of a Cytoplasmic Cell-Cycle Factor
explain: Cytoplasm from a Xenopus oocyte undergoing meiosis was injected into an immature oocyte. The recipient underwent premature germinal-vesicle breakdown and entered meiosis, showing that a transferable cytoplasmic factor can drive maturation. Figure focus: The donor oocyte is at germinal-vesicle-breakdown stage; cytoplasm is extracted and injected into an immature oocyte.
mustKnow: The experiment transferred cytoplasm between Xenopus oocytes.
Injected cytoplasm triggered premature meiotic entry.
A soluble cytoplasmic factor controls maturation.

terms.meaning: Breakdown of the oocyte nucleus as meiosis resumes.
Cytoplasmic activity that drives entry into M phase.
A frog genus widely used in cell-cycle experiments.

diagramGuide: The donor oocyte is at germinal-vesicle-breakdown stage; cytoplasm is extracted and injected into an immature oocyte.
Premature germinal-vesicle breakdown in the recipient proves a transferable cytoplasmic maturation-promoting activity.

interaction.q: What conclusion follows when cytoplasm from a maturing Xenopus oocyte triggers germinal-vesicle breakdown in an immature oocyte?
options: A transferable cytoplasmic factor promotes meiotic maturation
The donor nucleus contains a unique chromosome
interaction.explanation: The activity is carried in transferred cytoplasm, demonstrating a cytoplasmic maturation-promoting factor.

title: Cyclin-CDK Activity Across the Cell Cycle
explain: Different cyclin-CDK complexes dominate at different transitions. Cyclin E–CDK2 promotes the G1-to-S transition, Cyclin A with CDK1/CDK2 acts through S and G2, and Cyclin B–CDK1 drives M phase. Figure focus: Left ring maps checkpoints to G1-S, G2-M, and metaphase-anaphase transitions.
mustKnow: Cyclin E–CDK2 peaks around G1/S.
Cyclin A–CDK activity spans S and G2.
Cyclin B–CDK1 controls entry into M phase.

terms.meaning: A regulatory protein whose level changes during the cell cycle.
A cyclin-dependent kinase that phosphorylates cell-cycle targets.
Commitment point for entering DNA synthesis.

diagramGuide: Left ring maps checkpoints to G1-S, G2-M, and metaphase-anaphase transitions.
Right graph shows sequential cyclin-CDK waves: Cyclin E-CDK2, Cyclin A-CDK1/CDK2, then Cyclin B-CDK1.

interaction.q: Which cyclin-CDK complex peaks latest in the diagram?
interaction.explanation: Cyclin B-CDK1 rises in G2 and peaks in M phase.

title: RB1 Controls the G1-to-S Checkpoint
explain: Active, hypophosphorylated pRb binds and inhibits E2F transcription factors, preventing premature S-phase entry. Loss of both RB1 copies removes this control, allowing uncontrolled proliferation and predisposing to retinoblastoma and other cancers. Figure focus: Read the causal chain: hypophosphorylated pRb binds E2F -> S-phase genes stay off; loss of both RB1 copies -> E2F control is lost -> proliferation.
mustKnow: Active pRb blocks E2F.
pRb controls the G1-to-S checkpoint.
Loss of both RB1 copies removes cell-cycle restraint.
RB1 loss is linked to retinoblastoma.

terms.meaning: A tumor-suppressor gene encoding the pRb cell-cycle regulator.
A family of transcription factors that promotes S-phase gene expression.
The active form of pRb that binds and inhibits E2F.

diagramGuide: Read the causal chain: hypophosphorylated pRb binds E2F -> S-phase genes stay off; loss of both RB1 copies -> E2F control is lost -> proliferation.
The named primary tumor is retinal; osteosarcoma and soft-tissue sarcoma are additional risks.

interaction.q: Why does hypophosphorylated pRb suppress G1-to-S progression?
options: It binds and inhibits E2F transcription factors
interaction.explanation: Active pRb restrains E2F-dependent transcription needed for S phase.

title: Apoptosis Reference
explain: The slide points to Gerald Karp's Cell and Molecular Biology as the reference for deeper coverage of apoptosis. Figure focus: This is a bibliography slide with no new pathway diagram.
mustKnow: Use the reference only when a slide concept needs clarification; the examinable framework remains the apoptosis sequence and pathways presented here.

terms.meaning: A source for expanded explanation beyond the lecture slide.

diagramGuide: This is a bibliography slide with no new pathway diagram.
Retain the cited author/textbook only if your exam tests references.

interaction.q: Which author is cited for detailed apoptosis reading?
interaction.explanation: The reference slide cites Cell and Molecular Biology by Gerald Karp.

title: Stem Cells, Differentiation, and Apoptosis
explain: This title slide introduces the lecture's three connected themes: cells that self-renew, acquisition of specialized cell identity, and regulated cell removal. Figure focus: This is the title slide for stem cells, differentiation, and apoptosis.
mustKnow: The lecture links stem-cell potency, differentiation, and cell fate.

terms.meaning: An unspecialized cell capable of self-renewal and differentiation.
Acquisition of a specialized cell structure and function.

diagramGuide: This is the title slide for stem cells, differentiation, and apoptosis.
The salamander image signals regeneration but supplies no labeled mechanism.

interaction.q: Which three themes are named in the lecture title?
interaction.explanation: Those three topics appear directly in the section title.

title: Hematopoietic Differentiation Tree
explain: The diagram shows a multipotent hematopoietic stem cell branching into common myeloid and common lymphoid progenitors. These branches generate red cells, platelets, granulocytes, monocytes/macrophages, B cells, T cells, and natural killer cells. Figure focus: Start at the multipotent hematopoietic stem cell and split into common myeloid versus common lymphoid progenitors.
mustKnow: One hematopoietic stem cell can generate multiple blood-cell types.
The first major branches are myeloid and lymphoid progenitors.
B cells, T cells, and natural killer cells arise from the lymphoid branch.
Erythrocytes, megakaryocytes, granulocytes, and monocytes arise from the myeloid branch.

terms.meaning: A multipotent stem cell that produces blood-cell lineages.
A precursor for erythroid, megakaryocyte, granulocyte, mast-cell, and monocyte lineages.
A precursor for B, T, and natural killer cell lineages.

diagramGuide: Start at the multipotent hematopoietic stem cell and split into common myeloid versus common lymphoid progenitors.
Trace terminal branches: megakaryocyte -> thrombocytes; monocyte -> macrophage; B lymphocyte -> plasma cell; lymphoid branch also yields T and NK cells.

interaction.q: Which lineage relationship is shown correctly?
interaction.explanation: The diagram places macrophages downstream of monocytes in the myeloid branch.

title: Development Before Birth
explain: This linked video introduces the developmental journey from a fertilized egg to a multicellular organism. Figure focus: The video is developmental overview, not a labeled still.
mustKnow: Development transforms one fertilized cell into many organized, specialized cell types.

terms.meaning: The ordered process by which an organism grows and forms specialized tissues.

diagramGuide: The video is developmental overview, not a labeled still.
Use the subsequent slides for testable stages: zygote, cleavage/blastulation, gastrulation, and differentiation.

interaction.q: Which event converts a solid morula-like cell mass into a structure with a fluid-filled cavity?
interaction.explanation: Blastulation produces the blastocyst/blastula and its cavity.

title: Beating Cardiomyocytes in Culture
explain: The linked example shows differentiated heart-muscle cells beating in a culture dish. Their contraction is a visible specialized function acquired through differentiation. Figure focus: The field shows cultured cardiomyocytes; beating demonstrates acquisition of a specialized muscle-cell function.
mustKnow: Cardiomyocytes are differentiated cells specialized for contraction.
A specialized phenotype can be observed in cultured cells.

terms.meaning: A heart-muscle cell specialized for contraction.
Growth and maintenance of cells under controlled laboratory conditions.

diagramGuide: The field shows cultured cardiomyocytes; beating demonstrates acquisition of a specialized muscle-cell function.
Functional contraction is stronger differentiation evidence than cell shape alone.

interaction.q: Spontaneous beating in cultured cells is functional evidence of differentiation into what cell type?
interaction.explanation: Contractile beating is a specialized function of heart muscle cells.

title: What Is Differentiation?
explain: Differentiation converts unspecialized cells into cells with distinct structures and functions. Nerve cells conduct signals, muscle cells generate force, and red blood cells transport oxygen, yet all ultimately descend from the zygote. Figure focus: Read the vertical direction as normal development from zygote/blastocyst to organism; the reverse arrow represents experimental reprogramming.
mustKnow: Differentiation creates specialized morphology and physiology.
Different cell types perform different functions.
All cell types of the organism originate from the zygote.

terms.meaning: The single fertilized egg cell from which the organism develops.
The process by which an unspecialized cell becomes specialized.

diagramGuide: Read the vertical direction as normal development from zygote/blastocyst to organism; the reverse arrow represents experimental reprogramming.
Bottom branches show pluripotent cells directed toward ectoderm, mesoderm, or endoderm by different signals.

interaction.q: Which pairing of differentiated cell and principal function is correct?
interaction.explanation: The slide uses oxygen transport, conduction, and contraction as specialized examples.

title: Fate, Potency, Determination, and Differentiation
explain: Cell fate is what a cell normally becomes. Potency is the range of cell types it could become. Development progressively restricts potency. Determination commits a cell to a fate before visible specialization, and differentiation later produces the recognizable specialized phenotype. Figure focus: Treat the terms as a sequence: potency is what a cell can become; determination fixes a fate before visible change; differentiation produces the specialized phenotype.
mustKnow: Fate means the normal developmental outcome.
Potency means the range of possible outcomes.
Determination precedes visible differentiation.
Development usually reduces potency over time.

terms.meaning: The cell type a cell will normally become.
The range of cell types a cell can potentially generate.
Commitment to a developmental fate before visible specialization.
Execution of a specialized cell program and phenotype.

diagramGuide: Treat the terms as a sequence: potency is what a cell can become; determination fixes a fate before visible change; differentiation produces the specialized phenotype.
A determined cell may still resemble undetermined neighbors morphologically.

interaction.q: A cell has committed to a muscle fate but still resembles neighboring cells. Which term best describes it?
interaction.explanation: Determination fixes developmental fate before the visible specialized phenotype appears.

title: Hierarchy of Developmental Potency
explain: Stem-cell potency narrows through a hierarchy. Totipotent cells can form all embryonic and supporting tissues needed for an organism; pluripotent cells can form the body's many tissue types but not a complete organism; multipotent and oligopotent cells are progressively more lineage restricted; unipotent cells generate one cell type. Figure focus: Order categories by decreasing breadth: totipotent -> pluripotent -> multipotent -> oligopotent -> unipotent.
mustKnow: Totipotent has the broadest potential.
Pluripotent cells form many body cell types but not a whole organism by themselves.
Multipotent and oligopotent cells are lineage restricted.
Unipotent cells generate one cell type.

terms.meaning: Able to generate all embryonic and extraembryonic cell types needed for a complete organism.
Able to generate cell types from all major body lineages but not a complete organism alone.
Able to generate several cell types within a limited lineage range.
Able to generate only one mature cell type.

diagramGuide: Order categories by decreasing breadth: totipotent -> pluripotent -> multipotent -> oligopotent -> unipotent.
Use definitions rather than the slide's questionable example assigning hematopoietic stem cells to pluripotency; standard biology classifies them as multipotent.

interaction.q: Which potency class can produce several cell types within one lineage but not all body tissues?
interaction.explanation: Multipotent cells have a lineage-restricted but multi-cell-type output.

title: Clonality and Clonal Expansion
explain: A clone is a group of cells descended from one original cell. Clonal expansion occurs when that founder cell repeatedly divides, producing many genetically related descendants. Figure focus: Follow one lymphocyte clone: diversity is generated first, one antigen-matching clone is selected, and that clone expands.
mustKnow: Clonality traces cells back to one founder.
Clonal expansion increases the number of descendants from that founder.

terms.meaning: A population of cells descended from one original cell.
Repeated division that enlarges a clone.

diagramGuide: Follow one lymphocyte clone: diversity is generated first, one antigen-matching clone is selected, and that clone expands.
Cells labeled 2 share specificity; expansion increases number, not receptor diversity.

interaction.q: After an antigen selects lymphocyte clone 2, what changes during clonal expansion?
options: The antigen specificity of each clone-2 receptor
The identity of the selecting antigen
The genome of every unrelated clone
interaction.explanation: Expansion produces many descendants with the selected specificity.

title: Differentiation from a Totipotent Starting Cell
explain: The slide emphasizes that early totipotent cells begin with broad potential and generate increasingly specialized descendants through differentiation. Figure focus: The tree narrows from one high-potency state at the apex to many fixed differentiated endpoints at the base.
mustKnow: Differentiation moves cells from broad potential toward specialized identity.
Totipotency is associated with the earliest embryonic cells.

terms.meaning: Progressive narrowing of the cell types a developing cell can produce.

diagramGuide: The tree narrows from one high-potency state at the apex to many fixed differentiated endpoints at the base.
The arrows encode an inverse relation: differentiation increases downward while potency decreases.

interaction.q: Moving from the apex toward the base of the diagram represents what paired change?
options: Decreasing gene expression in every lineage
Increasing apoptosis and decreasing cell number only
interaction.explanation: Development narrows potential as cells acquire specialized identities.

title: Differential Gene Expression Drives Differentiation
explain: Differentiated cells behave differently because they express different subsets of genes. Different gene-expression patterns produce different protein sets, which create different structures and functions even though cells generally contain the same genome. Figure focus: Compare heat-map color patterns between progenitor groups rather than reading every gene name.
mustKnow: Differentiation depends on differential gene expression.
Different expressed genes produce different protein complements.
Cell identity is determined by which genes are active, not by wholesale replacement of the genome.

terms.meaning: Activation of different gene subsets in different cells.
The set of proteins present in a cell under particular conditions.

diagramGuide: Compare heat-map color patterns between progenitor groups rather than reading every gene name.
Different rows changing between cell types illustrate differential gene expression producing different protein sets.

interaction.q: What does a difference in heat-map pattern between MEP and LMPP primarily represent?
options: Different subsets of genes being expressed
Different chromosome numbers in every cell
interaction.explanation: Differentiation changes transcriptional programs while generally retaining the genome.

title: Blastulation
explain: Blastulation is an early developmental stage in which cleavage-stage cells organize into a blastula or blastocyst with a fluid-filled cavity. In mammals, this stage separates the inner cell mass from the outer trophoblast. Figure focus: Follow cleavage from few blastomeres to morula and then blastocyst.
mustKnow: Blastulation follows early cleavage divisions.
It produces a hollow early embryo.
The mammalian inner cell mass gives rise to the embryo proper.

terms.meaning: An early embryo organized around a fluid-filled cavity.
The mammalian blastula containing an inner cell mass and outer trophoblast.
The fluid-filled cavity of the blastula.

diagramGuide: Follow cleavage from few blastomeres to morula and then blastocyst.
In the blastocyst diagram, outer trophoblast surrounds the blastocoel; the inner cell mass sits asymmetrically inside.

interaction.q: Which structure gives rise to embryonic stem-cell cultures?
interaction.explanation: Embryonic stem cells are derived from the blastocyst's inner cell mass.

title: Inner Cell Mass and Embryonic Stem Cells
explain: The inner cell mass of the mammalian blastocyst contains cells that form the embryo proper. Embryonic stem-cell lines can be derived from these cells and retain pluripotency under suitable culture conditions. Figure focus: The XYClone laser is shown as a tool for isolating the inner cell mass.
mustKnow: Embryonic stem cells are associated with the inner cell mass.
Inner-cell-mass cells contribute to the embryo proper.
Embryonic stem cells are pluripotent.

terms.meaning: The blastocyst cell group that gives rise to the embryo proper.
A pluripotent cell derived from the early embryo and maintained in culture.

diagramGuide: The XYClone laser is shown as a tool for isolating the inner cell mass.
Embryonic stem-cell derivation uses inner-cell-mass cells, not trophoblast or blastocoel fluid.

interaction.q: What is the stated purpose of the XYClone laser in this context?
options: Excision of the inner cell mass
interaction.explanation: The slide labels the device for inner-cell-mass excision.

title: Gastrulation
explain: Gastrulation reorganizes the early embryo and establishes the primary germ layers. These layers later generate the tissues and organs of the body. Figure focus: Left diagram labels trophoblast, blastocoel, and inner cell mass before gastrulation; right sequence shows coordinated cell spreading/inward movement.
mustKnow: Gastrulation reorganizes the blastula-stage embryo.
Gastrulation establishes ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm in triploblastic animals.

terms.meaning: Early embryonic reorganization that establishes primary germ layers.
An early embryonic tissue layer that produces defined sets of organs.

diagramGuide: Left diagram labels trophoblast, blastocoel, and inner cell mass before gastrulation; right sequence shows coordinated cell spreading/inward movement.
Gastrulation reorganizes a hollow embryo and establishes germ layers rather than simply increasing cell number.

interaction.q: Which process transforms the blastula organization toward distinct germ layers?
interaction.explanation: Gastrulation reorganizes embryonic cells and establishes germ layers.

title: Gastrulation Video Reinforcement
explain: This linked video visualizes the cell movements that reorganize the early embryo during gastrulation. Figure focus: The historical video frame introduces classic embryology experiments.
mustKnow: Gastrulation uses coordinated cell movement to establish germ-layer organization.

terms.meaning: Coordinated movement of cells that changes embryonic form.

diagramGuide: The historical video frame introduces classic embryology experiments.
Treat it as context for transplantation/fate experiments discussed around slides 241-244.

interaction.q: Classic transplantation experiments in embryology primarily test which property?
options: Whether cell fate is autonomous or environment-dependent
interaction.explanation: Moving embryonic cells reveals whether their developmental behavior persists in a new environment.

title: Testing Whether Cell Behavior Is Retained
explain: The slide asks whether cells preserve their characteristic developmental behavior outside the original embryo. This motivates transplantation and culture experiments that test whether a cell's behavior is intrinsic, imposed by its environment, or both. Figure focus: The bright sheet spreading over the blastocoel roof is the behavior being tested outside the original embryo.
mustKnow: Cell behavior can be tested by changing the cell's environment.
Retention of behavior outside the embryo supports a stable internal developmental state.

terms.meaning: Behavior maintained by properties within the cell itself.
External signals and neighboring tissues that influence cell behavior.

diagramGuide: The bright sheet spreading over the blastocoel roof is the behavior being tested outside the original embryo.
Persistence after transplantation/culture supports a stable determined state; altered behavior would support environmental instruction.

interaction.q: If transplanted cells continue their original spreading behavior in a new embryo, what is the strongest inference?
options: Their developmental state is stably determined
interaction.explanation: Persistence despite a changed environment supports stable determination.

title: The Three Germ Layers
explain: Gastrulation establishes germ layers. Endoderm contributes to the digestive tract, liver, and pancreas; mesoderm contributes to kidney, cartilage, bone, spleen, and circulatory and lymphatic systems; ectoderm contributes to hair, nails, nervous system, and retina. Figure focus: Organize the text into a three-column map: ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm and their derivatives.
mustKnow: Endoderm: digestive tract, liver, pancreas.
Mesoderm: bone, cartilage, kidney, blood-associated systems.
Ectoderm: nervous system, retina, hair, and nails.
Diploblasts have two primary layers; triploblasts have three.

terms.meaning: Inner germ layer that forms much of the digestive tract and associated organs.
Middle germ layer that forms muscle, bone, blood, kidney, and related tissues.
Outer germ layer that forms the nervous system and external body structures.
Having ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm.

diagramGuide: Organize the text into a three-column map: ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm and their derivatives.
The slide distinguishes diploblasts (two layers) from triploblasts such as mammals (three layers).

interaction.q: Which derivative is matched to the correct germ layer?
interaction.explanation: The slide assigns digestive tract, liver, and pancreas to endoderm.

title: Till and McCulloch Bone-Marrow Experiment
explain: Whole-body irradiation damaged the mice's blood-forming system. Intravenous bone-marrow transplantation rescued survival in proportion to the number of marrow cells injected, supporting the presence of rare, consistently represented marrow cells with regenerative capacity. Figure focus: Top flow is experimental design: irradiate mice -> inject graded bone-marrow doses -> measure survival.
mustKnow: The recipients were whole-body irradiated mice.
Bone-marrow cells were injected intravenously.
More injected marrow cells correlated with greater survival.
The result supported a rare regenerative cell population in marrow.

terms.meaning: Tissue containing blood-forming stem and progenitor cells.
Restoration of blood-cell production after damage.
Radiation treatment used here to destroy endogenous blood-forming cells.

diagramGuide: Top flow is experimental design: irradiate mice -> inject graded bone-marrow doses -> measure survival.
In the left graph, survival changes with injected cell number; this dose-response supports rare regenerative units in marrow.

interaction.q: Which experimental result supports the existence of rare regenerative cells in marrow?
options: Survival falls as marrow dose rises
Survival rises with the number of injected marrow cells
All irradiated mice survive without injection
interaction.explanation: A marrow-cell dose-response is consistent with transplantable regenerative units.

title: Mauro and the Muscle Satellite Cell
explain: Electron microscopy of frog muscle revealed satellite cells next to muscle fibers. Mauro proposed that these cells were either precursors capable of producing muscle cells or remnants of embryonic development; later work established their role as muscle stem cells. Figure focus: The TEM shows a small satellite cell positioned beside a frog muscle fiber.
mustKnow: Satellite cells were identified by microscopy in muscle.
They were proposed as possible muscle-cell precursors.
Satellite cells are associated with muscle regeneration.

terms.meaning: A muscle-associated stem cell that can generate muscle-lineage cells.
Transmission electron microscopy, used to view cell ultrastructure.
A cell capable of producing a more differentiated descendant.

diagramGuide: The TEM shows a small satellite cell positioned beside a frog muscle fiber.
The 1961 interpretation offered two alternatives: muscle precursor or embryonic remnant; later evidence supports the precursor/stem-cell role.

interaction.q: Where was the satellite cell observed in Mauro's experiment?
interaction.explanation: Transmission electron microscopy identified the small cell beside muscle tissue.

title: Defining Properties of Stem Cells
explain: Stem cells combine long-term proliferative capacity with self-renewal and differentiation. Their output depends on their potency: embryonic stem cells generate all body cell types, while tissue-specific adult stem cells generate cells of their own tissue. Many adult stem cells spend time in a low-activity quiescent state. Figure focus: Group the list into defining capacities (self-renewal, differentiation, long-term proliferation) and physiological state (often quiescent).
mustKnow: Stem cells self-renew.
Stem cells generate differentiated descendants.
Adult stem cells reside in tissues and usually have restricted output.
Many stem cells can remain quiescent.

terms.meaning: Division that preserves the stem-cell population.
A reversible low-activity, non-dividing state.
A tissue-resident stem cell that maintains or repairs a limited set of cell types.

diagramGuide: Group the list into defining capacities (self-renewal, differentiation, long-term proliferation) and physiological state (often quiescent).
Contrast broad ESC output with tissue-restricted adult stem-cell output.

interaction.q: Which property distinguishes self-renewal from ordinary differentiation?
options: Production of only terminally specialized cells
Permanent exit into G0 in every division
Loss of proliferative potential after one cycle
Production of daughter cells that retain stem-cell identity
interaction.explanation: Self-renewal maintains the stem-cell pool.

title: Mature Cells Can Be Reprogrammed
explain: The slide highlights the 2012 Nobel Prize awarded to John B. Gurdon and Shinya Yamanaka for showing that mature cells can be reprogrammed to a pluripotent state. Differentiation is therefore not necessarily an irreversible loss of genetic potential. Figure focus: The two portraits are John Gurdon and Shinya Yamanaka; the citation is the 2012 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
mustKnow: Gurdon and Yamanaka shared the 2012 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
Their work showed that mature cells can be reprogrammed.
Reprogrammed mature cells can regain pluripotency.

terms.meaning: Resetting a differentiated cell's gene-expression state toward an earlier developmental potential.
Acquisition of pluripotent properties by a previously differentiated cell.

diagramGuide: The two portraits are John Gurdon and Shinya Yamanaka; the citation is the 2012 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
The shared concept is reprogramming mature cells to pluripotency by two different experimental routes.

interaction.q: Which pairing of scientist and experimental strategy is correct?
options: Gurdon - somatic-cell nuclear transfer; Yamanaka - transcription-factor reprogramming
Gurdon - Annexin V staining; Yamanaka - bone-marrow transplantation
Gurdon - GPCR crystallography; Yamanaka - cyclin discovery
Gurdon - teratoma removal; Yamanaka - gastrulation imaging
interaction.explanation: The Nobel recognized two routes demonstrating nuclear/cellular reprogramming.

title: Gurdon's Somatic Cell Nuclear Transfer
explain: Gurdon transferred nuclei from differentiated tadpole intestinal cells into enucleated Xenopus eggs. A small fraction developed into normal tadpoles, showing that a differentiated nucleus can still contain the genetic information needed to direct an entire organism when reset by egg cytoplasm. Figure focus: Follow source boxes into the enucleated Xenopus egg, then read the developmental outcome.
mustKnow: The donor nucleus came from differentiated intestinal epithelium.
The recipient was an enucleated Xenopus egg.
Some transplants produced normal tadpoles.
Differentiation does not normally delete the genome needed for development.

terms.meaning: Transfer of a body-cell nucleus into an egg whose nucleus has been removed.
An egg cell from which the nucleus has been removed.
Resetting a differentiated nucleus to support an earlier developmental program.

diagramGuide: Follow source boxes into the enucleated Xenopus egg, then read the developmental outcome.
The one-nucleolus mutation is a lineage marker proving offspring nuclei came from the differentiated donor rather than residual egg nucleus.

interaction.q: Why was the one-nucleolus mutation useful in Gurdon's experiment?
options: It served as a pluripotency factor
It marked descendants of the donor nucleus
interaction.explanation: The nucleolus phenotype tracked the genetic origin of resulting tadpoles.

title: Dolly the Sheep
explain: Dolly was produced by somatic cell nuclear transfer using a nucleus from an adult mammary cell and an enucleated egg. Her birth demonstrated that an adult somatic nucleus can be reprogrammed to support mammalian development. Figure focus: The TIME cover identifies Dolly and the year 1997.
mustKnow: Dolly was produced by somatic cell nuclear transfer.
The donor nucleus came from an adult somatic cell.
An enucleated egg provided the reprogramming cytoplasm.
Dolly provided mammalian evidence for nuclear reprogramming.

terms.meaning: The first mammal cloned from an adult somatic-cell nucleus.
An organism or cell population derived from one genetic source.
The nucleus of a non-germline body cell.

diagramGuide: The TIME cover identifies Dolly and the year 1997.
Dolly is the mammalian extension of somatic-cell nuclear reprogramming, not an iPSC experiment.

interaction.q: Which cell component from the adult donor was transferred to generate Dolly?
options: A complete adult mammary cell with its membrane
interaction.explanation: Dolly was made by transferring an adult somatic nucleus into an enucleated egg.

title: Induced pluripotent stem cells: the Yamanaka factors
explain: Yamanaka reprogrammed differentiated mouse fibroblasts into stem-cell-like cells by delivering selected transcription-factor genes with retroviral vectors. The minimum four-factor combination was Oct3/4, Sox2, c-Myc and Klf4, often abbreviated OSKM. Figure focus: Follow the boxes: differentiated mouse embryonic fibroblasts + retroviral candidate genes -> stem-cell-like colonies.
mustKnow: iPSCs are differentiated cells reprogrammed back to a pluripotent state.
The four Yamanaka factors are Oct3/4, Sox2, c-Myc and Klf4.
The starting cells shown are mouse embryonic fibroblasts.

terms.meaning: Induced pluripotent stem cell made by reprogramming a differentiated cell.
Oct3/4, Sox2, Klf4 and c-Myc.
A modified virus used here to deliver reprogramming genes into cells.
Able to produce nearly every cell type of the body.

diagramGuide: Follow the boxes: differentiated mouse embryonic fibroblasts + retroviral candidate genes -> stem-cell-like colonies.
The micrographs compare ES cells, an iPS clone, and parental MEFs; colony morphology shifts toward ES-like appearance after reprogramming.

interaction.q: Which factor set is sufficient in the slide's minimum reprogramming combination?
options: Cyclin E, Cyclin A, Cyclin B, CDK1
interaction.explanation: These four transcription factors form the OSKM reprogramming set.

title: How the four reprogramming factors were identified
explain: The graphs show a stepwise elimination experiment. Researchers began with 24 candidate factors, removed factors one at a time, narrowed the active set to 10, and then tested smaller combinations. Loss of colony formation identified factors required for reprogramming, leading to the four-factor OSKM set. Figure focus: Panel A removes one of 24 factors, panel B removes one of a narrowed 10, and panel C tests three-, two-, and four-factor mixtures.
mustKnow: Candidate factors were narrowed by systematic removal and colony-count assays.
A sharp fall in colonies after removing a factor indicates that factor is important.
Four factors were sufficient; two- or three-factor combinations were much less effective.

terms.meaning: A test that counts groups of successfully reprogrammed, proliferating cells.
A gene tested for a possible role in reprogramming.
Removing one factor from a mixture to test whether it is required.

diagramGuide: Panel A removes one of 24 factors, panel B removes one of a narrowed 10, and panel C tests three-, two-, and four-factor mixtures.
A sharp colony decrease on factor removal implies necessity; retained colonies after reduction imply sufficiency of the remaining combination.

interaction.q: If removing candidate factor 14 leaves colony number unchanged, what does that result suggest under the tested conditions?
options: Factor 14 is not essential in that mixture
interaction.explanation: A factor whose removal does not reduce colonies is dispensable in that tested combination.

title: Tests used to validate iPSCs
explain: A useful iPSC line should retain a normal chromosome set and show pluripotency. A normal karyotype checks chromosome number and structure. Teratoma formation after transplantation is a classic functional test because a teratoma can contain tissues derived from multiple germ layers. Figure focus: Left image is a karyotype for chromosome integrity; right panels show tissues such as heart, gut, liver, gonad, neural tube, and skin in a teratoma.
mustKnow: Karyotyping checks chromosome number and large structural abnormalities.
Teratoma formation is evidence that candidate iPSCs can form diverse tissue types.
Genetic stability and pluripotency are separate properties and both must be checked.

terms.meaning: An ordered display of a cell's chromosomes.
A tumor containing several tissue types, used experimentally as a pluripotency test.
Ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm, which generate the body's tissues.

diagramGuide: Left image is a karyotype for chromosome integrity; right panels show tissues such as heart, gut, liver, gonad, neural tube, and skin in a teratoma.
The two tests answer different questions: genetic stability versus multilineage differentiation capacity.

interaction.q: Which test answers whether candidate iPSCs can generate derivatives of multiple germ layers?
interaction.explanation: A teratoma containing varied tissues is a functional multilineage differentiation assay.

title: Why iPSCs changed biomedical research
explain: iPSCs avoid many ethical issues associated with obtaining embryonic stem cells and can be made from a particular patient. They enable patient-specific disease models, drug screening on relevant differentiated cells, and possible gene correction followed by replacement of diseased tissue. Figure focus: Group applications into modeling/testing (patient disease models, drug screens) and future intervention (gene correction, tissue engineering, transplantation).
mustKnow: iPSCs provide an alternative to embryonic stem cells.
Patient-derived iPSCs can model that patient's disease.
Directed differentiation produces target cells for drug testing.
CRISPR plus iPSCs offers a possible route to gene correction and cell replacement.

terms.meaning: A laboratory system that reproduces important features of a disease.
Guiding stem cells toward a chosen mature cell type.
Repairing a disease-causing DNA sequence.
Combining cells and materials to build or restore tissue.

diagramGuide: Group applications into modeling/testing (patient disease models, drug screens) and future intervention (gene correction, tissue engineering, transplantation).
Patient-derived iPSCs preserve the donor genotype while directed differentiation supplies the disease-relevant cell type.

interaction.q: Which application specifically depends on retaining a patient's genetic background?
interaction.explanation: Patient-derived iPSCs carry the donor genotype for disease modeling and drug testing.

title: Starting optic-cup development from embryonic stem cells
explain: Mouse embryonic stem cells were grown as a three-dimensional embryoid body under conditions that favor retinal development. Matrix proteins supplied structural support, while Activin promoted the retinal-field gene Rx. GFP made Rx-positive regions visible as spherical outgrowths. Figure focus: Read the timeline Day 1 -> Day 5 -> Day 7 -> Day 9: ES aggregate -> Rx-positive neuroepithelium -> evagination/spherical vesicle -> invagination and neural-retina/RPE pattern.
mustKnow: Activin was used to induce Rx expression.
Rx-positive cells were visualized by GFP.
The culture produced spherical evaginations that begin optic-cup morphogenesis.

terms.meaning: A three-dimensional aggregate of pluripotent stem cells that can begin organized differentiation.
A transcription factor important in early eye and retinal development.
Green fluorescent protein used as a visible reporter of gene expression.
A protein-rich matrix that supports three-dimensional cell growth.

diagramGuide: Read the timeline Day 1 -> Day 5 -> Day 7 -> Day 9: ES aggregate -> Rx-positive neuroepithelium -> evagination/spherical vesicle -> invagination and neural-retina/RPE pattern.
Green signal is Rx-GFP; red/blue outlines mark apical-basal organization in the schematic.

interaction.q: Which treatment was used to promote expression of the retinal-field gene Rx?
interaction.explanation: The slide states that Activin was used to induce Rx expression.

title: Self-organization into an optic cup
explain: The Rx-positive vesicles change shape over time without being manually sculpted. By about day 9, the initially spherical retinal tissue bends inward and develops the characteristic cup-like architecture of the early eye. Figure focus: Compare Day 7 spherical vesicle with Day 9 cup; green Rx-GFP identifies retinal tissue throughout.
mustKnow: Rx-positive spherical vesicles develop into optic cups.
The characteristic cup shape appears at approximately day 9.
The experiment demonstrates self-organizing morphogenesis in a 3D culture.

terms.meaning: The biological process that generates tissue shape and structure.
Outward bulging of a tissue layer.
Inward folding of a tissue layer.

diagramGuide: Compare Day 7 spherical vesicle with Day 9 cup; green Rx-GFP identifies retinal tissue throughout.
The shape change is self-organized morphogenesis, not manual folding.

interaction.q: At what approximate time does the Rx-positive structure display the characteristic optic-cup shape?
interaction.explanation: The Day 9 panels show the cup-shaped morphology.

title: Neural retina and pigment epithelium separate
explain: Different parts of the optic vesicle acquire different marker profiles. The invaginating distal layer expresses neural-retina markers such as Chx10 together with Rx and Pax6. The proximal outer layer expresses markers including Mitf and Otx2 and later becomes pigmented, resembling retinal pigment epithelium. Figure focus: Follow phases 1-4 from spherical vesicle through distal flattening, flexure, and apically convex invagination.
mustKnow: Distal invaginated tissue becomes neural retina.
The outer proximal epithelium becomes retinal pigment epithelium (RPE).
Chx10 marks neural-retina progenitors; Mitf and Otx2 support RPE identity.
Pigmentation of the outer layer is visible by about day 12.

terms.meaning: A marker associated with neural-retina progenitor cells.
Retinal pigment epithelium, the pigmented support layer outside the neural retina.
A transcription factor associated here with RPE development.
A transcription factor with a central role in eye development.

diagramGuide: Follow phases 1-4 from spherical vesicle through distal flattening, flexure, and apically convex invagination.
Distal invaginated layer carries neural-retina markers (Chx10, Rx, Pax6); proximal outer shell carries RPE markers and pigments by Day 12.

interaction.q: Which marker most specifically identifies the neural-retina progenitor side in the slide?
interaction.explanation: Chx10 is listed with Rx and Pax6 in the distal neural-retina layer; Mitf/Otx2 characterize the RPE side.

title: Host–pathogen interaction
explain: This lecture introduces how host defenses detect and eliminate infectious agents and how pathogens enter, attach, evade immunity and damage the host. Figure focus: This is the title slide for host-pathogen interaction.
mustKnow: Host–pathogen interaction includes both immune defense and microbial disease mechanisms.

terms.meaning: The organism in or on which another organism lives.
A microbe capable of causing disease.

Use it as a section boundary; specific immune-cell lineages begin on the next slide.

title: Where blood cells form
explain: Blood-cell production is called hematopoiesis. In adults, it occurs mainly in bone marrow. Lymphocytes also mature or become activated in lymphoid organs such as the thymus, lymph nodes, spleen and tonsils. Figure focus: Locate primary blood-cell production in bone marrow, then distinguish lymphoid tissues shown around the body.
mustKnow: Adult blood cells are produced mainly in bone marrow.
The thymus is important for T-cell maturation.
The spleen and lymph nodes are lymphoid organs, not the primary source of all blood cells.

terms.meaning: Formation of blood cells from stem and progenitor cells.
Soft tissue inside bones and the main adult site of blood-cell production.
An organ where immune cells develop, reside or respond to antigens.

diagramGuide: Locate primary blood-cell production in bone marrow, then distinguish lymphoid tissues shown around the body.
Thymus supports T-cell maturation; lymph nodes, spleen, and tonsils organize immune-cell residence/activation rather than making all blood cells.

interaction.q: Which organ shown is the principal adult site of hematopoiesis?
interaction.explanation: Adult blood-cell production occurs mainly in bone marrow; the other labeled organs are lymphoid sites.
